name: Topical estrogen (estriol) cream

card.summary: A weak estrogen cream discussed for skin thickness; menopausal skin data exist, appearance-use data are thin.
card.note: Hormone product; generally prescription-only, with estrogen-class effects.

quick.overview:
Estriol is a mild natural estrogen used mainly in menopausal therapy. Creams are promoted for skin thickness and collagen.

Wikipedia reports research showing it can reverse postmenopausal skin thinning; facial appearance trials in other groups were not found.
quick.mechanism: Estriol activates estrogen receptors but more weakly than estradiol, acting as a partial agonist.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated; reported effects include breast tenderness and local irritation. Like other estrogens it can cause endometrial hyperplasia. It is generally prescription-only.

lead: Estriol (E3) is a weak natural estrogen, one of the three major human estrogens alongside estradiol and estrone, used mainly in menopausal hormone therapy. It is sold as tablets, vaginal creams and suppositories and as skin creams, some over the counter and some from compounding pharmacies.[1][2]

In appearance circles, topical estriol is discussed as a way to counter the thinning and loss of collagen that skin undergoes after menopause, with the aim of firmer, thicker, smoother-looking skin. Wikipedia reports that research has found estriol can reverse the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen content.[2]

A 1996 controlled clinical trial in the International Journal of Dermatology examined topical estrogen treatment (0.01% estradiol and estriol preparations) for skin aging in perimenopausal women, prompted by the coincidence of menopausal symptoms and the onset of skin aging.[3] Most other published clinical work on estriol concerns menopausal symptoms and vaginal tissue rather than facial appearance.[4][5]
Estriol as a medicine is generally prescription-only, and as an estrogen it carries estrogen-class effects.

chain: Thicker skin with more collagen, firmer and smoother looking (reported in postmenopausal skin)
angle.text: Topical estriol is used by some people to restore skin thickness and collagen after the estrogen decline of menopause, aiming for firmer, smoother skin. Evidence reported for this comes from postmenopausal skin.

Generally prescription-only; some skin creams OTC or compounded[2]

paras: Estriol skin creams are marketed over the counter and by compounding pharmacies for aging skin.[2] The stated goal is to restore skin thickness, collagen content and firmness lost after menopause.[2][3]
Topical creams are one of the forms of estriol listed on Wikipedia alongside oral tablets, vaginal creams, suppositories and pessaries and intramuscular injection.[2]

Estriol is used for menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes, vaginal atrophy and painful intercourse, and has been linked to fewer urinary tract infections; vaginal use is well established, with much higher vaginal than oral bioavailability. Its effects on bone density are described as inconsistent.[2] Reviews of estriol's clinical benefits and of ultra-low-dose estriol vaginal gels in postmenopausal women have been published.[4][5]

Estriol has also been marketed in a combined product with lactobacilli for vaginal atrophy and urinary tract infections.[2] A 2024 Maturitas randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial examined an ultra-low-dose 0.005 percent estriol vaginal gel for preventing urinary tract infections in postmenopausal women with genitourinary syndrome of menopause,[5] and a 2020 phase II randomized trial studied the same gel for vulvovaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women with early breast cancer treated with aromatase inhibitors.[6] A 2025 randomized trial examined vaginal microbiota with radiofrequency and topical estriol in menopausal genitourinary syndrome.[7]

Estriol is generally well tolerated. Reported effects include breast tenderness and local irritation, burning, itching or discharge with vaginal use. Like other estrogens it can cause endometrial hyperplasia, though typical vaginal doses appear to carry little of this risk.[2]

Estrogens are contraindicated in breast and endometrial cancer, and Wikipedia notes some evidence that estriol may stimulate the growth of active breast cancer.[2] Oral estriol in women with a uterus has traditionally been paired with a progestogen, while typical vaginal doses do not appear to carry a meaningful hyperplasia risk.[2] Estrogens are considered relatively safe in acute overdose, with possible nausea, vomiting and vaginal bleeding.[2]

Estriol is an agonist at both ER-alpha and ER-beta, with binding affinity of about 11 to 14 percent (ER-alpha) and 18 to 21 percent (ER-beta) of estradiol's. At very high concentrations it antagonises the membrane receptor GPER, unlike estradiol, which activates it.[2] It is a partial agonist and can weakly mimic estradiol or partly block it when both are present, an effect linked to its short receptor occupancy of roughly 1 to 6 hours versus 6 to 24 hours for estradiol.[1][2]

Oral bioavailability is about 1 to 2 percent, because most of the dose is sulfated on first pass, while vaginal bioavailability is about 10 to 20 percent. Protein binding is about 92 percent, mostly to albumin; metabolism is by glucuronidation, sulfation, oxidation and hydroxylation, and over 95 percent is excreted in urine as conjugates.[2] Estriol binds poorly to sex hormone-binding globulin.[1] Wikipedia reports that oral estriol does not appear to change breast density, liver proteins, lipids or clotting parameters at the doses studied.[2]

Outside pregnancy, estriol circulates at nearly undetectable levels and is made in small amounts in the liver. During pregnancy the placenta produces it in very large amounts, and its level rises about 1,000-fold, making it the most abundant estrogen in a pregnant woman.[1] Reviews of estrogen biology describe estrogen as a regulator of metabolism in brain and body and of musculoskeletal tissue after menopause.[8]

Estriol was discovered in 1930, isolated and purified from the urine of pregnant women by Marrian and colleagues, and was introduced for medical use shortly afterward.[1][2] It was first sold in the 1930s as oral capsules under brands such as Theelol (Parke-Davis) and Estriol (Lilly, Abbott), and later as tablets under names including Gynasan, Hormomed, Ovestin and Ovo-Vinces.[2] A 1978 JAMA letter on estriol and a 1968 German review show its clinical use was discussed in the mid-twentieth century.[9][10]

Today it is generally prescription-only, less commonly used than estradiol or conjugated estrogens but widely available in Europe and elsewhere, with Ovestin as the main brand. Topical creams are sold over the counter or made by compounding pharmacies. Estriol under the brand Incurin is also used in veterinary medicine for urinary incontinence in dogs.[2] Measuring unconjugated estriol in maternal blood is part of prenatal triple and quadruple screening tests.[1]

A 1996 controlled clinical trial in perimenopausal women examined whether topical estrogen (0.01% estradiol and estriol preparations) could reverse some changes of aging skin.[3] Wikipedia states that research shows estriol reverses the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen.[2] No studies were found testing estriol cream for facial appearance in non-menopausal users.
Other published estriol trials concern vaginal and urogenital outcomes rather than skin: the 2024 and 2020 vaginal gel trials above enrolled postmenopausal women.[5][6]
